newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean court sentences 110 students in crackdown.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean court sentences 110 students in crackdown.

text.p: A South Korean court on Tuesday jailed 51 students and gave suspended prison terms to 59 others for their part in violent pro-North Korean campus protests in August, court officials said.

The sentences were part of a crackdown on a student movement that backed President Kim Young-sam's rise to power, but which authorities say has since been hijacked by North Korea and which Kim has now branded a "terrorist" threat to national security.
The verdicts were the first from the trials of 444 students following the violence at Seoul's prestigious Yonsei University.
Fifty-one students were given jail terms of eight months to three years for taking part in an illegal protest, engaging in acts of violence and obstructing officials in their duty.
The others were handed suspended jail sentences of between one and 1-1/2 years.
Presiding judge Min Hyong-ki told the court the protests had "benefitted the enemy", state media reported.
"These protests hampered social stability, and a stern application of the law is inevitable," he said. "We cannot glorify contraventions of law and order in the name of unification."
The judge said the sentences were a warning against violent protests that cause "enormous human and property damage".

Riot police stormed Yonsei to end the occupation of two teaching blocks by students who were taking part in an annual pro-Korean unification rally and protesting the presence of 37,000 U.S. troops in South Korea.
One riot policeman died in pitched fighting.
One of the teaching blocks that was smashed beyond repair by students with iron bars has been reopened as a museum of violence.
On Monday, police arrested the leader of the radical student group Hanchongryon, which led the Yonsei demonstrations. Park Byoung-un, 23, was held along with 23 others.

Seoul maintains it is committed to unification, but authorities accused the students of embracing North Korea's plan to leave intact both Pyongyang's communist system and Seoul's democratic government.
Police produced stacks of North Korean propaganda that they said had been seized from the students.
North and South Korea are still technically at war since the 1950-53 Korean conflict was ended by a truce, not a ceasefire.
North Korea has denounced the action against student demonstrators.
